claims.text: Croup is diagnosed clinically; labs and imaging are not routine.
claims.quote: Laboratory studies and imaging are not routinely recommended.

claims.text: If the diagnosis is uncertain: AP and lateral neck and chest X-rays; a steeple sign supports croup.
claims.quote: If there is diagnostic uncertainty, patients should have AP and lateral radiographs of the neck and chest; subepiglottic narrowing ( steeple sign ) seen on AP neck radiographs supports the diagnosis

claims.text: Suspected epiglottitis: direct inspection, typically in the operating room.
claims.quote: Direct inspection (typically in the operating room)

claims.text: Suspected foreign body: inspiratory and expiratory chest X-rays, or chest CT in some centers.
claims.quote: If foreign body aspiration is suspected, chest radiograph with inspiratory and expiratory views should be done (or in some centers a chest CT).

claims.text: Structural cause: CT of the neck and chest; direct laryngoscopy finds vocal fold and structural problems.
claims.quote: Direct laryngoscopy can detect vocal fold abnormalities, structural abnormalities, and tumors, and it can be performed in conjunction with securing an airway. CT of the neck and chest should be performed if there is concern about a structural abnormality, such as an upper airway tumor or tracheomalacia.
